data.title: Hero
data.tagline: Use the opening area to explain the page's main point and next step
data.description: The Hero usually sits directly below the Header or Navbar. It may combine a headline, supporting copy, a primary action, and a product visual, but there is no required component checklist. What matters is that these elements explain the page's main value together. Customer logos, feature lists, and pricing are normally separate sections even when they appear nearby.

lessonPractice.title: A first-time visitor opens a product site and needs to understand the problem it solves and what to do next. How should the hero work?

options.label: State the value in a clear heading and explanation, emphasize one action, and show the necessary product view
options.feedback: The heading, support copy, action, and visual serve one primary understanding so visitors can judge relevance and continue.

options.label: Use an abstract slogan and large decorative image, explaining the actual capability near the page bottom
options.feedback: The composition may be striking, but new visitors cannot tell what the product does or whether to continue.

options.label: Place customer logos, every feature, three prices, and the FAQ together in the hero
options.feedback: Important content does not all belong in the hero. Too many parallel messages dilute the primary value and action.

data.agentPrompt: Redesign the site hero: state who the product helps and what problem it solves, clarify the outcome in support copy, emphasize one primary CTA, and use a real product view as evidence. Keep features, pricing, and FAQ in later sections, then run a five-second comprehension check.

references.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
